items.question: Suppose $X_1$ and $X_2$ are subspaces of a vector space $V$, and let $u \in X_1$, $v \in X_2$. Explain why the sum $u + v$ must belong to the set $X_1 + X_2$, using the definition of $X_1 + X_2$ implied in the sources.
items.referenceAnswer: By definition, $X_1 + X_2 = \{ u + v \mid u \in X_1,\, v \in X_2 \}$. Since $u \in X_1$ and $v \in X_2$, their sum $u + v$ is explicitly an element of $X_1 + X_2$.

items.question: Let $X_1 = \{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_n\}$ and $X_2 = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\}$ be subspaces of $V$. Why does closure under scalar multiplication for $X_1$ imply that $\alpha_i u_i \in X_1$ for all scalars $\alpha_i$ and all $i$? Justify using the subspace criteria given.
items.referenceAnswer: Since $X_1$ is a subspace, it is closed under scalar multiplication: for any $u_i \in X_1$ and any scalar $\alpha_i$, the product $\alpha_i u_i$ must also be in $X_1$. This is directly stated as a property of subspaces in the source.

items.question: Given $u = a_1 u_1 + \cdots + a_n u_n + b_1 v_1 + \cdots + b_n v_n$ and $v = c_1 u_1 + \cdots + c_n u_n + d_1 v_1 + \cdots + d_n v_n$, where all $u_i \in X_1$, $v_j \in X_2$, show that $\alpha u + \beta v$ can be written as a linear combination of vectors from $X_1 \cup X_2$. What does this imply about $[X_1 \cup X_2]$?
items.referenceAnswer: Expanding $\alpha u + \beta v$ yields $\sum_{i=1}^n (\alpha a_i + \beta c_i) u_i + \sum_{i=1}^n (\alpha b_i + \beta d_i) v_i$, which is a linear combination of vectors in $X_1 \cup X_2$. Hence $\alpha u + \beta v \in [X_1 \cup X_2]$, confirming closure under linear combinations — a key step in proving $[X_1 \cup X_2]$ is a subspace.

items.question: The source states that $[X_1 \cup X_2]$ is a subspace of $V$. Using only the information provided, explain why this span must contain all finite linear combinations of vectors from $X_1$ and $X_2$.
items.referenceAnswer: By definition, the span $[X_1 \cup X_2]$ is the set of all finite linear combinations of vectors in $X_1 \cup X_2$. Since $X_1$ and $X_2$ are sets of vectors (and subspaces), any such combination — e.g., $p_1 u_1 + \cdots + p_n u_n + q_1 v_1 + \cdots + q_n v_n$ — lies in $[X_1 \cup X_2]$, as shown in the algebraic derivation.

items.question: Suppose $u_i, u_j \in X_1$, where $X_1$ is a subspace of $V$. Why must $u_i + u_j$ also belong to $X_1$? Use the subspace axioms referenced in the source.
items.referenceAnswer: Because $X_1$ is a subspace, it is closed under vector addition: for any two elements $u_i, u_j \in X_1$, their sum $u_i + u_j$ must also lie in $X_1$. This is explicitly stated as a consequence of $X_1$ being a subspace.
